description: Hoover, HUAC and the Rosenbergs — how Cold War anxiety reshaped American politics from 1947.
content_html:
Why Did Fear of Communism Grip America After 1945?

When the Second World War ended in 1945, Americans expected peace. Instead, a new and invisible enemy emerged: Communism. The Soviet Union, America’s wartime ally, was rapidly expanding its control over Eastern Europe. In 1949 it tested its first atomic bomb. That same year, Communist forces under Mao Zedong took power in China. To many Americans, Communism seemed to be advancing everywhere — and they feared it could infiltrate their own country from within.

Key Fact

Between 1947 and 1950, a series of shocks deepened the Red Scare: the Soviet atomic test (August 1949), the ‘loss’ of China to Communism (October 1949), the conviction of Alger Hiss for perjury (January 1950) and the start of the Korean War (June 1950).

Truman’s Loyalty Order and HUAC

President Harry Truman responded in March 1947 by issuing Executive Order 9835, known as the Loyalty Order. It required loyalty checks on all federal employees. Over the next five years, around 3 million government workers were investigated and several thousand dismissed or resigned. Truman wanted to head off Republican accusations that his administration was ‘soft’ on Communism.

Congress already had the HUAC — the House Un-American Activities Committee — which had been investigating radical organisations since 1938. In 1947 HUAC turned its attention to Hollywood, calling 19 screenwriters and directors to testify. Ten of them — the “Hollywood Ten” — refused to answer questions, citing the First Amendment. They were cited for contempt of Congress and jailed. Their names appeared on the Hollywood blacklist, ending their careers.

One of HUAC’s most dramatic moments came in August 1948. Whittaker Chambers, a former Soviet spy who had defected, testified that Alger Hiss — a senior State Department official — had passed him secret documents in the 1930s. Hiss denied it. A young Republican congressman named Richard Nixon pushed the investigation hard. Hiss was convicted of perjury in January 1950 and sentenced to five years in prison. The case convinced many Americans that Communists had reached the highest levels of government.

J. Edgar Hoover and the FBI

J. Edgar Hoover was the most powerful domestic security figure of the era. As FBI director, he had been building files on suspected radicals since the 1920s. From the late 1940s he fed information about suspected Communists to HUAC and to journalists, helping to shape public anxiety. Hoover believed that any association with the Communist Party — even a long-past membership — made a person a security risk. He testified frequently before Congress and cultivated a reputation as America’s indispensable anti-Communist guardian.

It is important to distinguish J. Edgar Hoover from Herbert Hoover, the president who served from 1929 to 1933. J. Edgar Hoover was never elected to anything — his power came from his position as FBI chief, which he held for 48 years.

In 1950 the FBI arrested Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, a New York couple, on charges of passing atomic bomb secrets to the Soviet Union. Julius had recruited a network of spies that included Ethel’s brother, David Greenglass, who worked at the Los Alamos nuclear laboratory. The Rosenbergs were convicted in March 1951 and executed on 19 June 1953 — the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case polarised the country: supporters claimed the evidence against Ethel was thin and that antisemitism influenced the prosecution; opponents saw the death sentences as a necessary deterrent. Declassified Soviet intelligence documents (the Venona decrypts) later confirmed Julius’s espionage; historians still debate the extent of Ethel’s direct involvement.

Key Fact

J. Edgar Hoover was FBI Director from 1924 to 1972. He fed intelligence on suspected Communists to HUAC and journalists, helping to build public hysteria long before Senator McCarthy rose to prominence.

Media Campaigns and American Values

The government and private organisations used the media to highlight what they presented as the differences between American democracy and Soviet Communism. Radio broadcasts, films and pamphlets promoted free enterprise, religious faith and individual liberty as uniquely American virtues that Communism threatened. The McCarran Internal Security Act 1950 went further, requiring Communist and Communist-front organisations to register with the Justice Department and barring their members from certain federal jobs and passports.
exam_tip_html: When writing about the Red Scare, give specific examples rather than general statements. Name J. Edgar Hoover (not Herbert Hoover), cite the Loyalty Order of 1947, and distinguish between HUAC’s role in Hollywood and the Alger Hiss case. In an “explain two reasons” question, each reason needs a concrete example and a clear explanation of the consequence — for instance, the Rosenberg execution illustrates how fear of atomic espionage made the Red Scare so intense. Examiners want identification, detail and consequence: all three in every point.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A series of shocks — the Soviet atomic test, the Communist victory in China, the Korean War — convinced many Americans that Communism was an urgent internal threat as well as an external one.
  • Truman’s Loyalty Order, HUAC investigations and J. Edgar Hoover’s FBI turned anti-Communism into official government policy, creating a climate of suspicion that damaged civil liberties.
  • The Rosenberg case and the Hollywood blacklist showed how the Red Scare affected ordinary lives; the Venona evidence later confirmed some espionage fears, but the scale of the domestic threat was consistently exaggerated.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Hollywood blacklist during the Red Scare.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names the blacklist and gives specific detail, e.g. the Hollywood Ten refused to testify before HUAC and were jailed for contempt, their careers ending as a result. Secure: Names the blacklist with some correct detail. Developing: Vague reference to actors or writers losing jobs. Emerging: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of J. Edgar Hoover in the post-war Red Scare.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail). Mastering: Two well-supported features, e.g. (1) Hoover fed intelligence on suspected Communists to HUAC, helping committees build their cases; (2) he cultivated media relationships to generate public fear of internal subversion. Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the conviction of Alger Hiss in 1950 intensified the Red Scare.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes with specific detail and links them — Hiss had been a senior State Department official, so his conviction suggested Communists had reached the highest levels of government; this validated HUAC's claims and undermined trust in the administration; it gave credibility to further investigations. Secure: Explains one or two causes with clear detail and connection. Developing: Describes the case but does not explain its impact on public fear. Emerging: Brief or inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the US government used the Loyalty Order and HUAC investigations to respond to Communist concerns after 1947.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons each with evidence and explanation of how they contributed to the government response, e.g. (1) Truman needed to protect his administration from Republican charges of being 'soft' on Communism — the Loyalty Order showed decisive action; (2) HUAC exploited genuine fears from external shocks (Soviet bomb, Korea) to assert congressional authority over potential internal subversion. Secure: Two reasons developed with relevant evidence. Developing: Two reasons identified but limited development. Emerging: One weak reason.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Rosenberg case in shaping American attitudes towards Communism in the early 1950s?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced analysis covering multiple dimensions of significance — it reinforced fears of atomic espionage; it showed the government would impose the ultimate penalty; it generated controversy (supporters questioned the fairness of the trial, especially regarding Ethel) revealing how the Red Scare divided society; later Venona evidence confirmed Julius's role. Compares significance to other factors (Hiss case, HUAC, Soviet bomb). Secure: Clear argument about significance with relevant evidence. Developing: Describes the case but analysis of significance is limited. Emerging: Narrative only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the main causes of the post-war Red Scare in the USA in the years 1947 to 1953.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained analytical essay covering multiple causes — external shocks (Soviet bomb 1949, China 1949, Korean War 1950) creating genuine security concerns; political opportunism (Republicans attacking Truman; Hoover building FBI power); institutional mechanisms (HUAC; Loyalty Order; McCarran Act) amplifying fear; specific cases (Hiss, Rosenbergs) providing focal points for anxiety. Integrated argument with well-chosen evidence throughout. Secure: Several causes with evidence; some sustained analysis. Developing: Describes causes with limited analysis or explanation of how they combined. Emerging: Brief narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: What position did J. Edgar Hoover hold that gave him so much power during the Red Scare?
In what year were Julius and Ethel Rosenberg executed?
President Truman issued the _____ in March 1947, requiring background checks on all federal government employees.
The ten Hollywood figures who refused to testify before HUAC and were jailed for contempt became known as the Hollywood _____.
Match each person to their role in the post-war Red Scare:
right: Former Soviet spy who testified against Hiss
HUAC member who pushed the Hiss investigation
State Department official convicted of perjury

flashcard_questions.a: Truman's 1947 Loyalty Order requiring background checks on all federal employees.
Ten screenwriters and directors jailed for contempt after refusing to testify before HUAC.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Alger Hiss convicted of in January 1950?
flashcard_questions.a: Perjury — lying under oath about passing documents to Soviet spy Whittaker Chambers.
A US signals intelligence project that decrypted Soviet messages, later confirming Julius Rosenberg's espionage.

flashcard_questions.q: Which two external events in 1949 dramatically heightened American fear of Communism?
flashcard_questions.a: The Soviet atomic test (August) and the Communist victory in China (October).

flashcard_questions.q: What did the McCarran Internal Security Act 1950 require?
flashcard_questions.a: Communist and Communist-front organisations to register with the Justice Department.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it important to distinguish J. Edgar Hoover from Herbert Hoover?
flashcard_questions.a: J. Edgar Hoover was FBI Director; Herbert Hoover was a former US president — confusing them is a common exam error.

flashcard_questions.q: What role did Richard Nixon play in the Hiss case?
flashcard_questions.a: As a Republican HUAC member, he pushed the investigation that led to Hiss's conviction.

glossary_terms.definition: A political movement seeking to abolish private property and establish state ownership of industry, associated with the Soviet Union.
A 1947 presidential directive requiring background checks on all federal employees to screen out Communist sympathisers.
The House Un-American Activities Committee, a congressional body that investigated suspected Communist influence in American institutions from 1938 onwards.
Director of the FBI from 1924 to 1972, who used the bureau to investigate and undermine groups he considered subversive.
A sweeping federal law of 1950 that required members of Communist and Communist-front organisations to register with the government.
